lesson.title: The Baseline That Makes Comparison Possible: The Control Group
lesson.summary: A control group is the group that does not receive the treatment being tested, providing the baseline outcome without which a treatment group's results cannot be interpreted or attributed to the treatment.
lesson.body:
A control group is the group of experimental units in an experiment that does not receive the treatment being tested, or that receives a standard baseline treatment such as a placebo, existing therapy, or no intervention at all. Its purpose is to provide a baseline outcome to compare against the treatment group's outcome, so that any difference between the two groups can be attributed to the treatment rather than to outside factors that would have affected everyone regardless.

Without a control group, an experiment has no baseline, and there is no way to know whether an observed outcome in the treatment group reflects the treatment's real effect or simply what would have happened anyway. Suppose 50 headache subjects take a new pain reliever and 70% report feeling better within an hour. That number alone is uninterpretable, since headaches often improve on their own within an hour regardless of any treatment, and some of that 70% may reflect the placebo effect discussed earlier rather than the drug's chemistry. A control group of subjects who receive a placebo pill under identical conditions supplies the missing baseline: if 45% of the control group also reports feeling better within the hour, then the drug's estimated genuine effect is closer to 70 minus 45, which is 25 percentage points, not the full 70 percentage points.

Consider a full experiment with 200 headache subjects, randomly split into 100 who receive the real drug and 100 who receive a placebo, with both groups treated identically in every other respect. If 71 of the 100 drug subjects improve within an hour, 71%, and 44 of the 100 placebo subjects, the control group, also improve, 44%, the difference, 27 percentage points, is the estimated effect attributable specifically to the drug. Random assignment ensures the two groups started out similar in age, headache severity, and every other lurking variable researchers did not explicitly control for, so this 27 point gap is a far more trustworthy estimate of the drug's true effect than the raw 71% figure alone.

A control group does not always mean a placebo group. In some experiments the control group receives the current standard treatment rather than an inert placebo, particularly when withholding all treatment would be unethical, so that the new treatment is judged against the best existing option rather than against doing nothing. Either way, the logic is identical to what makes a well-designed experiment more trustworthy than an observational study in the first place: comparison against a defined baseline group is what allows a difference in outcomes to be attributed to the treatment.

A control group and random assignment work together. Randomly assigning subjects to treatment and control groups is what makes the two groups comparable to begin with, and the control group is what gives the treatment group something meaningful to be compared against. Neither piece alone is enough, together they form the backbone of the principle explored fully in the next section, comparison in experiments.
